themes.name: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK

cards.title: Patron Saints of the UK
cards.hook: Four nations, four saints: George, Andrew, David, Patrick — each with a feast day to remember.

cards.title: Churches of the UK
cards.hook: The monarch heads the Church of England; Wales and Northern Ireland have no established church at all.

cards.title: King James Bible & the Puritans
cards.hook: King James I authorised an English Bible; the Puritans wanted worship stricter and plainer still.

cards.title: Christmas & Boxing Day
cards.hook: The 25th celebrates the birth of Christ; the 26th, Boxing Day, keeps the holiday going.

cards.title: Easter, Lent & Good Friday
cards.hook: Forty days of Lent lead to Good Friday and to Easter, always in March or April.

cards.title: Hogmanay & the New Year
cards.hook: Scotland calls 31 December Hogmanay, and Auld Lang Syne sings in the New Year.

cards.title: Diwali & Eid al-Fitr
cards.hook: Diwali is the Festival of Lights; Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan’s month of fasting.

cards.title: Halloween & April Fool's Day
cards.hook: Ghosts come out on 31 October; the newspapers print jokes until midday on 1 April.

cards.title: Bank Holidays
cards.hook: When the banks close and much of Britain closes with them, that is a bank holiday.

cards.title: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe
cards.hook: Every summer Edinburgh fills with festivals, and the Fringe is the biggest of them all.

cards.title: Flowers & Foods of the Nations
cards.hook: Daffodil, thistle, shamrock — and haggis or an Ulster Fry to taste the nations.

cards.title: UK Currency: Coins & Banknotes
cards.hook: Everything runs on pounds sterling — and Scottish and Northern Irish notes spend anywhere in the UK.

cards.title: Working in the UK
cards.hook: Prove your identity and your right to work, and the DWP issues your National Insurance number.

cards.title: School Governors
cards.hook: Governors set a school's strategic direction and keep watch on its performance.

cards.title: Everyday Rules in the UK
cards.hook: Licence at 17, moped at 16, alcohol at 18 — and every dog's collar names its owner.

cards.title: UK Charities
cards.hook: The National Trust minds Britain's places; Friends of the Earth minds the environment.

cards.title: William Shakespeare
cards.hook: England’s greatest playwright began life in the market town of Stratford-upon-Avon.

cards.title: Wordsworth & The Daffodils
cards.hook: A poet inspired by nature, Wordsworth made the daffodil the most famous flower in English poetry.

cards.title: Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales
cards.hook: Pilgrims riding to Canterbury told stories on the way — Chaucer turned them into poems.

cards.title: Great British fiction
cards.hook: Sherlock Holmes, The Lord of the Rings and the Booker Prize — landmarks of British fiction.

cards.title: The Cenotaph, Whitehall
cards.hook: The war memorial in Whitehall where the King and politicians gather for Remembrance Day.

cards.title: Wren’s St Paul’s & Crathes Castle
cards.hook: From the ashes of 1666 rose Wren’s St Paul’s; in Scotland stands Crathes Castle.

cards.title: British stars of the screen
cards.hook: From Chaplin’s silent tramp to Oscar nights, British actors made their mark in Hollywood.

cards.title: British film successes
cards.hook: Harry Potter, James Bond and Nick Park’s animations — British film is a global success story.

cards.title: The BBC & broadcasting rules
cards.hook: Funded by the licence fee, free of government control — and party coverage must be balanced by law.

cards.title: British art & design
cards.hook: Hockney’s pop art, Cliff’s Art Deco ceramics, the Tate in London and the Turner Prize.

cards.title: Music & theatre in Britain
cards.hook: Elgar at the Proms, the Beatles in the sixties and the West End’s Theatreland.

cards.title: British inventors & scientists
cards.hook: Radar, the web, the Turing machine, split atoms and DNA — British minds led the way.

cards.title: Churchill & Florence Nightingale
cards.hook: The public’s greatest Briton of all time, and the nurse who founded modern nursing.

cards.title: The UK & Great Britain
cards.theme: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK
cards.hook: Great Britain means England, Scotland and Wales; add Northern Ireland and you have the UK.

cards.title: Crown Dependencies & Overseas Territories
cards.theme: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK
cards.hook: Channel Islands and Isle of Man sit near; St Helena and the Falklands lie far — none of them is part of the UK.

cards.title: Capitals & Cities of the UK
cards.theme: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK
cards.hook: Beyond London: Edinburgh for Scotland, Cardiff for Wales, Belfast for Northern Ireland.

cards.title: Landmarks of London
cards.hook: Big Ben is the bell at Parliament, the Jewels sit in the Tower, and Whitehall keeps the Cenotaph.

cards.title: National Parks of Britain
cards.hook: Britain has 15 national parks, and England’s largest is the Lake District.

cards.title: Famous Places Around the UK
cards.hook: Stonehenge, the Giant’s Causeway, Skara Brae and the Eden Project — pin each one to its place on the map.

cards.title: Horse Racing in the UK
cards.hook: The Grand National runs at Aintree, Royal Ascot in Berkshire, and the Scottish Grand National at Ayr.

cards.title: Classic British Sporting Events
cards.hook: Match each event to its sport: the Ashes is cricket, the Six Nations is rugby, Wimbledon is tennis.

cards.title: Olympic & Paralympic Britain
cards.hook: The Games came to Britain in 1908, 1948 and 2012 — remember the Paralympic champions too.

cards.title: British Sporting Heroes
cards.hook: 1954: Bannister breaks the four-minute mile; 1966: Bobby Moore lifts the World Cup.

cards.title: The UK’s Diverse Population
cards.hook: About one person in ten in the UK has a parent or grandparent born outside the country.

cards.title: Responsibilities of UK citizens
cards.hook: Five duties, one theme: look after yourself, your family, your area, the law and other people's rights.

cards.title: Fundamental principles of British life
cards.hook: Democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance, participation – five pillars worth reciting.

cards.title: Parliament: Commons & Lords
cards.hook: Commons elected, Lords appointed – remember which house is which and who sits in each.

cards.title: MPs & the Speaker
cards.hook: MPs serve a place: everyone in the constituency, reachable by letter, phone or a local surgery.

cards.title: Ministers, civil servants & opposition
cards.hook: Home Secretary, home front: crime, policing and immigration all land on one desk.

cards.title: The UK constitution
cards.hook: There is no single document to read – the British constitution is famously unwritten.

cards.title: General elections & voting
cards.hook: Every 5 years a poll card arrives; when an MP quits mid-term, a by-election follows.

cards.title: Registering & standing for election
cards.hook: Eighteen opens the door to standing for office; Northern Ireland registers each voter individually.

cards.title: Margaret Thatcher
cards.hook: The Iron Lady claimed two records: first woman PM and longest-serving PM of the 20th century.

cards.title: Prime Ministers through history
cards.hook: From Walpole in 1721 to the 2010 coalition, the same office keeps changing hands.

cards.title: The role of the monarch
cards.hook: The monarch appoints the government but does not run it: advise, warn, encourage.

cards.title: What the devolved nations control
cards.hook: Devolved bodies run health and schools; defence and immigration never left London.

cards.title: The Senedd & NI Assembly
cards.hook: Remember 60 and 90: Senedd members and Northern Ireland MLAs, both elected proportionally.

cards.title: Juries in the UK
cards.hook: One register, two duties: it lets you vote and can call you, at random, to a jury at 18.

cards.title: Criminal courts & Youth Courts
cards.hook: Minor crime goes to magistrates – and in Youth Courts, young names stay out of the papers.

cards.title: Criminal vs civil law
cards.hook: If it harms the public it is criminal; workplace and money disputes stay civil.

cards.title: Solicitors & small claims
cards.hook: Time is money at a solicitor's office; small claims let you skip the lawyer entirely.

cards.title: Dealing with the police
cards.hook: A police complaint has many doors: the station, the Chief Constable or an independent body.

cards.title: Laws that protect people
cards.hook: The law reaches inside the home: partner violence, forced marriage and FGM are all crimes.

cards.title: Early Britain: Stone to Iron Age
cards.hook: Hunter-gatherers came first, farmers followed 6,000 years ago, and Iron Age kings put their names on the first coins.

cards.title: Roman Britain
cards.hook: Caesar tried first in 55 BC, Boudicca fought back, and Hadrian built a wall to keep out the Picts.

cards.title: Anglo-Saxons and the Vikings
cards.hook: After Rome left in AD 410 the Jutes, Angles and Saxons arrived; Alfred the Great later united England against the Vikings.

cards.title: William the Conqueror & 1066
cards.hook: One 1066 conquest left England a tapestry, a great survey and a tower — all pointing back to William.

cards.title: Magna Carta, 1215
cards.hook: 1215 is the year the law was set above the king.

cards.title: Battle of Bannockburn, 1314
cards.hook: 1314 at Bannockburn: Robert the Bruce’s Scots beat the English, and Scotland stayed unconquered.

cards.title: The Black Death, 1348
cards.hook: One arrival in 1348 — the plague called the Black Death — killed a third of England.

cards.title: Medieval England: War, Land, Language
cards.hook: A 116-year war with France, serfs on a lord’s land, and two languages merging into English.

cards.title: The Wars of the Roses
cards.hook: Two families, two roses: York against Lancaster.

cards.title: Henry VIII & the Reformation
cards.hook: A refused divorce led Henry VIII to break with the Pope and found the Church of England.

cards.title: Mary, Queen of Scots
cards.hook: Scotland turned Protestant in 1560, but its queen Mary Stuart stayed Catholic and was finally executed.

cards.title: Elizabeth I & the Spanish Armada
cards.hook: 1588 is the year Protestant England, under Elizabeth I, defeated the Armada Spain sent to restore Catholicism.

cards.title: The Early Stuarts & the Civil War
cards.hook: Divine right met Parliament's army — the king lost his head and England, briefly, its monarchy.

cards.title: Cromwell & the escape of Charles II
cards.hook: The man who ruled Britain without a crown — and the king who survived by hiding in an oak tree.

cards.title: Charles II & the Restoration
cards.hook: Charles II came back from the Netherlands to a reign of fire, refugees and new rights for prisoners.

cards.title: The Glorious Revolution, 1688
cards.hook: A king replaced without resistance, and a Bill that set the limits of royal power — 1688 changed the rules.

cards.title: Bonnie Prince Charlie & the Highlands
cards.hook: The last Stuart bid for the throne rose with the Highland clans; later the crofts were cleared for sheep.

cards.title: The Enlightenment
cards.hook: The 18th century rethought politics, philosophy and science — Smith on economics, Hume on human nature.

cards.title: Isaac Newton & gravity
cards.hook: One book, the Principia, showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

cards.title: The Industrial Revolution
cards.hook: Steam power made Britain the first country to industrialise — bringing canals, railways and new factory laws.

cards.title: 20th-century British inventions
cards.hook: Jet engines, television and Concorde — British invention did not stop with steam.

cards.title: Victorian free trade & the Great Exhibition
cards.hook: Import taxes fell and the Crystal Palace rose — free-trade Britain put itself on display in 1851.

cards.title: Ireland in the 19th century
cards.hook: A failed potato crop cost a million lives, while Fenians pressed for complete independence from the UK.

cards.title: American colonies win independence
cards.hook: Tax colonists who have no say in Parliament and you may lose them — in 1776, thirteen colonies left.

cards.title: Trafalgar & Waterloo
cards.hook: Nelson fell winning at Trafalgar; Wellington finished Napoleon at Waterloo, the last battle between Britain and France.

cards.title: Abolition of slavery
cards.hook: A politician's long campaign paid off in 1833, when the Emancipation Act freed the Empire's slaves.

cards.title: Exploration & the growing empire
cards.hook: Elizabethan settlers in America, Cook charting Australia — an empire built on trade, and contested with France.

cards.title: The Crimean War
cards.hook: Britain, Turkey and France against Russia — the first war the public followed in news stories and photographs.

cards.title: The Boer War, 1899-1902
cards.hook: Settlers from the Netherlands — the Boers — held off the British Empire in South Africa for over three years.

cards.title: The Suffragettes & Votes for Women
cards.hook: Pankhurst's suffragettes won the vote in steps — over-30s in 1918, equal at 21 in 1928 — with war work tipping the scales.

cards.title: The First World War
cards.hook: The assassination of Austria's Archduke in 1914 started it; the guns stopped at 11.00 am on 11th November 1918.

cards.title: The Second World War
cards.hook: Germany invaded Poland in 1939; the RAF fought the Battle of Britain and small boats helped rescue over 300,000 men at Dunkirk.

cards.title: Ireland: Home Rule to Republic
cards.hook: Home Rule was promised in 1913, put on hold by world war — and in 1949 Ireland became a republic.

cards.title: Admiral Nelson & Trafalgar
cards.hook: Nelson commanded the British fleet at Trafalgar against the combined French and Spanish fleet and was killed in the battle.

cards.title: The Great Depression in Britain
cards.hook: In the 1930s slump Britain's traditional heavy industries — shipbuilding above all — were hit hardest.

cards.title: Post-war Britain
cards.hook: Free secondary schools, a new United Nations, the Swinging Sixties and Concorde — how Britain changed from 1944 on.

cards.title: The Commonwealth
cards.hook: Most Commonwealth members were once part of the British Empire; they work together on democracy and development.

facts.statement: The patron saint of England is **St George**, celebrated on **23rd April**.

variants.stem: Who is the patron Saint of England?
variants.explanation: The patron Saint of England is St George .

variants.stem: When is St George’s day?
variants.explanation: St George’s day, patron of England is celebrated on the 23rd of April .

facts.statement: The name or photographs of a young person accused in a Youth Court **cannot be published in newspapers or used by the media**.

variants.stem: The names or photographs of young people found guilty of a crime can be published in newspapers or used by the media.
variants.explanation: False . Members of the public are not allowed in Youth Courts, and the name or photographs of the accused young person cannot be published in newspapers or used by the media .

facts.statement: Sir Edward Elgar is remembered because **he was a musician**, best known for the Pomp and Circumstance Marches.

variants.stem: What was Edward Elgar famous for?
variants.explanation: Sir Edward Elgar (1857-1934) was a musician . His best known work is probably the Pomp and Circumstance Marches. March No1 (Land of Hope and Glory) is usually played at the Last Night of the Proms at the Royal Albert Hall.

facts.statement: The Scottish Grand National takes place at **Ayr**.

variants.stem: Where does the Scottish Grand National take place?
variants.explanation: The Scottish Grand National takes place at Ayr .

facts.statement: The laws passed after the Glorious Revolution marked the beginning of the **constitutional monarchy**.

variants.stem: The laws passed after the Glorious Revolution marked the beginning of the ______.
variants.explanation: The laws passed after the Glorious Revolution marked the beginning of the constitutional monarchy .

facts.statement: The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679 and guaranteed **that every prisoner has a right to a court hearing**.

variants.stem: What did the Habeas Corpus Act introduce?
options: That every prisoner has a right to a court hearing
A salary for members of Parliament (MPs)
Financial help for the unemployed, old-age pensions and free school meals
Measures to improve the conditions of workers
variants.explanation: The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679. This was a very important piece of legislation which remains relevant today. Habeas corpus is Latin for ‘you must present the person in court’. The Act guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully. Every prisoner has a right to a court hearing.

facts.statement: The Proms is **an eight-week summer season of daily orchestral classical music concerts**, held in venues including the Royal Albert Hall.

variants.stem: What is “the Proms”?
options: An annual event that gives awards in a range of categories, such as best British group and best British solo artist
An annual cultural festival which includes music, dance, art and original performances largely in Welsh
An eight-week summer season of daily orchestral classical music concerts
Light-hearted plays with music and comedy
variants.explanation: The Proms is an eight-week summer season of orchestral classical music that takes place in various venues, including the Royal Albert Hall in London.

facts.statement: Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park is in the west of **Scotland**.

variants.stem: Where is Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park located?
variants.explanation: Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park is located in the west of Scotland .

facts.statement: Isaac Newton is famous for **the discovery of gravity**: his Principia Mathematica showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

variants.stem: What was Isaac Newton known for?
variants.explanation: Newton‘s most famous published work was Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (‘Mathematical Principle of Natural Philosophy’), which showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

variants.stem: What did Isaac Newton discover?
variants.explanation: Newton’s most famous published work was Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (‘Mathematical Principle of Natural Philosophy’), which showed how gravity applied to the whole universe. Newton also discovered that white light is made up of the colours of the rainbow.

facts.statement: The First World War came to an end **in 1918** — **at 11.00 am on 11th November 1918** — with victory for Britain and its allies.

variants.stem: When did the WWI come to an end?
variants.explanation: The World War I ended in 1918 .

variants.stem: When did the First World War end?
variants.explanation: The First World War ended at 11.00 am on 11th November 1918 with victory for Britain and its allies.

facts.statement: **Emperor Hadrian** built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts, ancestors of the Scottish people.

variants.stem: Who built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts (ancestors of the Scottish people)?
variants.explanation: The Emperor Hadrian built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts (ancestors of the Scottish people).

facts.statement: **The University of Oxford** and **the University of Cambridge** compete in a popular yearly rowing race on the River Thames.

variants.stem: Which two universities participate in an annual rowing race that takes place on the River Thames?
variants.explanation: Rowing is also popular, both as a leisure activity and as a competitive sport. There is a popular yearly race on the Thames between Oxford and Cambridge Universities .

facts.statement: The British constitution is **not written down in any single document**, which is why it is described as 'unwritten'.

variants.stem: Does Britain have a written constitution?
variants.explanation: The British constitution is not written down in any single document, and therefore it is described as ‘unwritten’ .

facts.statement: Boxing Day, the day after Christmas Day, is a public holiday on **26th December**.

variants.stem: When is Boxing Day celebrated?
variants.explanation: Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day (26th December) and is a public holiday.

facts.statement: Public holidays in the UK are known as **bank holidays**.

variants.stem: What is the name of the holiday when banks and many other businesses are closed for the day?
variants.explanation: There are public holidays each year called bank holidays , when banks and many other businesses are closed for the day.

variants.stem: How are public holidays called?
variants.explanation: There are public holidays each year called bank holidays , when banks and many other businesses are closed for the day.

facts.statement: To drive on public roads you need **a valid driving licence** and must be at least **17 years old** for a car or motorcycle.

variants.stem: What do you need to drive in the UK?
variants.explanation: In the UK, you must have a driving licence to drive on public roads.

variants.stem: What is the minimum age required to drive a motorcycle?
variants.explanation: In the UK, you must be at least 17 years to drive a car or motorcycle and you must have a driving licence to drive on public roads.

facts.statement: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe (‘the Fringe’) takes place in **Edinburgh**, Scotland, every summer.

variants.stem: Where does “the Fringe” festival take place?
variants.explanation: The Edinburgh Festival takes place in Edinburgh , Scotland, every summer. It is a series of different arts and cultural festivals, with the biggest and most well-known being the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (‘the Fringe’).

facts.statement: By law, radio and television coverage of political parties must be **balanced**, with **equal time** given to rival viewpoints.

variants.stem: By law, radio and television coverage of the political parties must be balanced and so equal time has to be given to rival viewpoints.
variants.explanation: This statement is true .

facts.statement: The **Cenotaph** is a war memorial located in Whitehall.

variants.stem: What is the name of the War Memorial located in Whitehall?
variants.explanation: The Cenotaph is a war memorial located in Whitehall.

facts.statement: The Northern Ireland Assembly has been **suspended on a few occasions** by the UK government.

variants.stem: The UK government has never suspended the Northern Ireland Assembly.
variants.explanation: False . The Northern Ireland Assembly has been suspended on a few occasions.

facts.statement: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished the Pope’s authority and Scotland established **a Protestant church** with an elected leadership.

variants.stem: What kind of church did Scotland establish in 1560?
variants.explanation: In 1560, the predominantly Protestant Scottish Parliament abolished the authority of the Pope in Scotland and Roman Catholic religious services became illegal. A Protestant Church of Scotland with an elected leadership was established but, unlike in England, this was not a state Church.

facts.statement: **London’s West End**, also called ‘Theatreland’, is particularly well known for its theatres.

variants.stem: Where is Theatreland?
variants.explanation: London’s West End , also known as ‘Theatreland’, is particularly well known for its theatres.

facts.statement: After the Great Fire of London in 1666, St Paul’s Cathedral was rebuilt to a design by the architect **Sir Christopher Wren**.

variants.stem: Who was the architect that rebuilt Saint Paul’s cathedral after the Great Fire in 1666?
variants.explanation: In 1666, a great fire destroyed much of the city, including many churches and St Paul’s Cathedral. London was rebuilt with a new St Paul\\\\\\\'s, which was designed by a famous architect, Sir Christopher Wren .

facts.statement: From 1853 to 1856 Britain fought with Turkey and France against **Russia** in the Crimean War.

variants.stem: Who did Britain fight against in the Crimean War?
variants.explanation: From 1853 to 1856, Britain fought with Turkey and France against Russia in the Crimean War.

facts.statement: You must be **18** to buy alcohol in the UK and **18** to go into betting shops or gambling clubs.

variants.stem: How old do you have to be to buy alcohol in the UK?
variants.explanation: It is a criminal offence to sell alcohol to anyone who is under 18 or to buy alcohol for people who are under the age of 18 . (There is one exception: people aged 16 or over can drink alcohol with a meal in a hotel or restaurant).

variants.stem: How old do you have to be to go into betting shops or gambling clubs?
variants.explanation: You have to be 18 to go into betting shops or gambling clubs.

facts.statement: The currency in the UK is the **pound sterling** (symbol £).

variants.stem: What is the name of the UK currency?
variants.explanation: The currency in the UK is the pound sterling (symbol £).

facts.statement: After the Norman Conquest, nobles spoke **Norman French** and peasants spoke **Anglo-Saxon**; these two languages combined into one English language.

variants.stem: Which two languages combined to become one English language?
variants.explanation: After the Norman Conquest, the king and his noblemen had spoken Norman French and the peasants had continued to speak Anglo-Saxon . Gradually these two languages combined to become one English language.

variants.stem: Which two languages were used across England during the Middle Ages?
variants.explanation: The Middle Ages saw the development of a national culture and identity. After the Norman Conquest, the king and his noblemen had spoken Norman French and the peasants had continued to speak Anglo-Saxon .

facts.statement: Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came to England from **France**.

variants.stem: Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came to England, which country did they come from?
variants.explanation: Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came from France .

facts.statement: **Wimbledon**, played each year at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, is the most famous tennis tournament in the UK.

variants.stem: What is the most famous tennis tournament played in the UK?
variants.explanation: The most famous tournament hosted in Britain is The Wimbledon Championships , which takes place each year at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club.

facts.statement: **April Fool‘s Day**, 1 April, is the day when jokes are published in newspapers and telecast on TV.

variants.stem: What is the day when jokes are published in newspapers and telecast on TV?
variants.explanation: April Fool‘s Day , 1 April, is a day when people play jokes on each other until midday. The television and newspapers often have stories that are April Fool jokes.

facts.statement: The World Wide Web was invented by **Sir Tim Berners-Lee**.

variants.stem: Who invented the World Wide Web?
variants.explanation: The inventor of the World Wide Web was Sir Tim Berners-Lee .

facts.statement: Civil servants are not political appointees – **they are chosen on merit and are politically neutral**.

variants.stem: How are civil servants appointed and what political party do they belong to?
options: They are chosen on merit and form part of the Liberal Democrats party
They are chosen randomly and form part of the Conservative party
They are chosen randomly and are politically neutral
They are chosen on merit and are politically neutral
variants.explanation: Civil servants are chosen on merit and are politically neutral – they are not political appointees.

variants.stem: Are civil servants appointed by the government?
variants.explanation: Civil servants are accountable to ministers. They are chosen on merit and are politically neutral – they are not political appointees .

facts.statement: The 'Dunkirk spirit' recalls **the evacuation of Allied soldiers from France during World War II**, when small boats helped the Navy rescue over 300,000 men.

variants.stem: What is known as the “Dunkirk spirit”?
options: When the German air force bombed London and other British cities at night-time
The evacuation of Allied soldiers from France during World War II
When new social classes appeared after the Black Death
The period when many refugees called Huguenots came from France
variants.explanation: During WWII as France fell, the British decided to evacuate British and French soldiers from France in a huge naval operation. Many civilian volunteers in small pleasure and fishing boats from Britain helped the Navy to rescue more than 300,000 men from the beaches around Dunkirk.

facts.statement: The BBC is funded by the TV licence fee and is **independent of government**.

variants.stem: Is the BBC controlled by the government?
variants.explanation: The BBC is the largest broadcaster in the world. It is the only wholly state-funded media organisation that is independent of government .

facts.statement: The UK has hosted **the Olympic games** on **3** occasions: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

variants.stem: Which of the following major sports event took place in the UK in 2012?
variants.explanation: The UK has hosted the Olympic games on three occasions: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

variants.stem: How many times has the UK hosted the Olympic games?
variants.explanation: The UK has hosted the Olympic games on three occasions: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

facts.statement: Charles I believed in the ‘Divine Right of Kings’ and tried **to rule without the Parliament**.

variants.stem: Charles I believed in the ’Divine Right of Kings’ so he tried:
options: To rule with the approval of the Parliament
To raise money for the Parliament
variants.explanation: Charles I believed in the ’Divine Right of Kings’: the idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule. He thought that the king should be able to act without having to seek approval from Parliament and he tried to rule without the Parliament .

facts.statement: The Union Flag, also known as the Union Jack, is **the Flag of the United Kingdom**.

variants.stem: What is the Union Jack?
options: The Flag of the United Kingdom
The shield used by British Knights
A trade union to protect workers rights
variants.explanation: The Union Flag, the Flag of the United Kingdom is also known as the Union Jack.

facts.statement: **Women in Britain today make up about half of the workforce.**

variants.stem: Which of the following statements is true:
options: Women in Britain today make up about half of the workforce.
Women in Britain today make up about one quarter of the workforce.
variants.explanation: Women in Britain today make up about half of the workforce .

facts.statement: The Northern Ireland Assembly has **90** elected members, known as MLAs, chosen **by a system of proportional representation**.

variants.stem: How many members does the Northern Ireland Assembly have?
variants.explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly has 90 elected members, known as MLAs (members of the Legislative Assembly).

variants.stem: How are the members of the Northern Ireland Parliament elected?
options: By a system of proportional representation
Using a system of ranked voting
Using the first past the post system
variants.explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly has 90 elected members, known as MLAs (members of the Legislative Assembly). They are elected with a form of proportional representation .

facts.statement: Towns, cities and rural areas in the UK are governed by **democratically elected councils**, often called 'local authorities'.

variants.stem: Towns, cities and rural areas in the UK are governed by government appointed officials.
variants.explanation: False .Towns, cities and rural areas in the UK are governed by democratically elected councils , often called ‘local authorities‘.

facts.statement: The Tate Britain and Tate Modern galleries are in **London**.

variants.stem: Where is the Tate Art Gallery located?
variants.explanation: The Tate Britain and Tate Modern are in London .

facts.statement: King James I’s new English translation of the Bible is called the King James Version or the **Authorised Version**.
